source_corrections.correction: Do not create a separate character named Ustasra solely from the local English capitalization at 737. It is a title; Sograt’s card incorporates the later vizier episode following the scholarly identification supplied by the root agent.
Sograt is explicitly named in chapter 2; his identification in chapters 31 and 35 is editorial and should retain the supporting lexical and scholarly note.
The current story graph places Rustaveli in Arabia. His card belongs to the authorial frame and must not imply that he lives in, visits, or acts within the Arabian plot.
Tinatin is a reigning sovereign after the opening coronation, not only a princess or a romantic prize.

English-to-Georgian stanza attachments can shift even in early chapters: the private-audience physical description is Georgian 123 but English attached to 124; Rostevan’s beard-tearing is Georgian 821 but English attached to 820. Use the chapter ranges as project locators and check Georgian for exact appearance citations.

The phrase 'sunlike' and the crystal/ruby/jet imagery often describe ideal beauty poetically. Such language must not be converted automatically into literal eye colors, complexion, height, or ethnicity.
Tamar, David, the prologue’s beloved, and names in the epilogue catalogue belong to framing or literary-reference scope. They should not silently expand the fictional story cast.

No rhetorical invocations of God, planets, philosophers, or sages are proposed as character cards. Collective armies, huntsmen, guards, and entertainers are likewise not split into invented individuals.
Current story_graph data contains 65 chapter_steps, rather than the 26 keyframe episodes mentioned in README.

English translations can be displaced relative to Georgian stanza_number: in chapter 8, black clothing appears in Georgian stanza 266, while its English rendering is attached to entry 263. Source locators here follow the checked Georgian text.
Chapter 62 English entries 1579–1588 render later enthronement material. Georgian stanza 1587 actually reports Parsadan’s death; Georgian stanzas 1594–1596 report Ramaz’s attack on India.
Chapter 63 English translations are null. The second Ramaz submission is supported by the actual Georgian text, including stanzas 1602–1618, rather than the generated English summary alone.
Asmat receives one seventh of India at Georgian chapter 64 stanzas 1649–1650. Her marriage appears at stanza 1653; the corresponding English narrative is not aligned to those entries.
The queen of India pardons Ramaz after Tariel’s request at Georgian chapter 64 stanzas 1642–1643; Tariel gives him gifts and imposes tribute at stanza 1648.

Chapter 50 generated summary incorrectly says the Kadjeti queen has returned. The text and surrounding letters establish that the queen and Kadjis have not yet returned, creating urgency before their arrival.
Tariel’s killing of the bridegroom is intentional and follows Nestan’s instructions. The plan to spare the army does not make the whole escape bloodless: Tariel also describes killing pursuers.
The original Khvarazmsha portrait/id identifies the visiting prince, while the marriage negotiations also contain the separate father called Khvarazmsha, ruler of Khwarazm.
Pridon is injured during a dispute with his cousins over an island. Saying Tariel restores an already lost throne goes beyond the checked text.
The treasure chamber supplies exceptional armor, but the inscription does not establish that the equipment was manufactured by the Kadjis; it refers to a possible conflict between Kadjis and Devis.
Davar’s Kadjeti connection and sorcery do not provide a literal witch outfit, facial features, or complexion.
Poetic comparisons to the sun, crystal, rubies, lions, and trees are not literal appearance specifications or evidence for a modern nationality or skin color.
